ebullient

/ih-BUL-yent/ - the stress falls on BUL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ebullient means bubbling over with cheerful enthusiasm.

Ebullient as ever, the debate coach burst in waving the tournament bracket like a winning lottery ticket.

Example

The astronomy-camp director is somehow ebullient at four in the morning — cheering every meteor, hugging her thermos, narrating the sky in three different voices — until the campers forget they are cold.

Ebullient literally means boiling over, and that is the picture: high spirits at a rolling boil, spilling onto everyone nearby. Its unit-mate effervescent is the lighter cousin — a fizz, a sparkle — where ebullient is the full, bubbling pot.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

exuberant: Exuberant is ebullient's nearest neighbor: overflowing energy and high spirits, visible from across a field. The shade of difference is the bubbling — ebullient keeps its boiling-over, spilling-onto-everyone quality, while exuberant can be athletic and wordless: a dog tearing joyful circles is exuberant without making a sound.

irrepressible: Irrepressible describes what happens when someone tries to hold the spirits down: they pop straight back up, however hard you press. It is about the resilience of a mood, not its volume. Ebullient is the volume — cheer boiling over onto everyone nearby, whether or not anyone has tried to squash it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

glum: low and silent

subdued: dialed down, energy deliberately kept quiet

Where it sits · how far the high spirits overflow

lively → ebullient → manic

lively vs. ebullient: Lively is bright, wide-awake energy, but it is milder than ebullient — nothing is overflowing yet.

manic vs. ebullient: Manic goes further than ebullient — ebullient energy is joyful and welcome; manic energy has tipped past control into frenzy.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-: out (Latin ex-)

Root — bull: to boil, bubble (Latin bullire)

Suffix — -ient: adjective ending: in a state of

Put it together: E- (out) + bull- (to boil) + -ient = boiling out, boiling over. Latin bullire, to bubble, also simmers inside bouillon — a broth made by boiling — and ebullition, chemistry's word for bubbling. An ebullient person is the human version: spirits at a rolling boil.

Use the root in a new word: bouillon: The last item on the shopping list was bouillon.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / vivid

Reach for ebullient when high spirits visibly overflow — a person, a mood, a whole locker room. It is warmer and more physical than enthusiastic. And keep it beside its unit-mate effervescent deliberately: effervescent charm fizzes and sparkles; ebullient energy boils and spills. One is champagne, the other a pot rattling its lid.
